We've already seen significant deleveraging and retail/institutional margin liquidations (maybe it continues for more time, who knows). 

But medium-long term, I'm not quite sure how anyone can be bearish the upstream semis or neoclouds. 

Given each hyperscaler has flagged either compute shortages, rising cloud demand + pricing power, or increased spending for chips/networking.  

My "bottleneck" thesis with many of these upstream semi supply chains is that when trillions in capital flows into things from InP substrates or memory (which were both treated as cheap commodities) or even energy. 

Lot of these current AI names that were treated as useless before in telecom cycles or even toilet sellers. 

Gets rerated when their inflection period hits and capex flows into their balance sheets. 

As seen with $NVDA GPUs past few years, memory this year, CPUs/MLCCs next few years, CPO in 2027, Glass Substrates in 2027, 800V in 2027, and so on.

My favorite non AI idea, I think this notoriously conservative conglomerate is still heavily sandbagging generational sales and profit impact of GTA 6 for FY26 (ending March 2027).

My focus is on gaming, but all the other wonderful businesses look really strong across the board with guidance raises for all but one segment.

GTA VI launches November 19. 112 days out and it lands inside Sony's fiscal year. Sony just guided full year gaming revenue up to $29.4B against $31.1B last year and sees profit climbing massively.

They are guiding gaming to SHRINK in the fiscal year that contains the biggest entertainment launch in history, to which they are the second biggest beneficiary of.

They raised gaming operating income by $388M and listed the reasons as tariff refunds, foreign exchange, cost improvements. Not one word about GTA VI or a major upcoming title.

Meanwhile $TTWO already put $8.0B to $8.2B of FY27 net bookings in writing, up from $6.7B. The platform collecting 20-30% of every dollar of 70% of that guide has its own gaming revenue going DOWN year over year.

That is before PS Plus reactivations and new sign ups and before the in-game purchases of the online economy, which ships day one this cycle instead of taking a while to build up like it did for GTA V.

$SONY also says that memory has been secured for their forecasted console demand this year and they won't expect a further change to profitability (so they won't be hiking prices further). My personal expectation is that PS5's will be impossible to buy this Holiday season, and we could even see front-loading happen this quarter.

Again this is just not a huge concern because profits are being guided up to over 39% growth. Sony's gaming business is getting more profitable amid the memory crunch because of all the network services revenue where the margin is (games, subscriptions). 

Risks are real though an earthquake just hit Japan that is disrupting their semiconductor factory that is a driver of their second most profitable business, but they expect it to come back online in August. This happened too recently to get baked into guidance. Also currency risk is material.

I'm personally holding Jan calls that are inching towards ITM. Already up 100% as of earlier today. Don't see reason to sell yet as it doesn't seem the market is putting two and two together yet on the GTA thesis.

I'm long $LITE. 

After July's carnage, $LITE is sitting -32% off its ATH. If you were only interested before, you might want to pay attention to this company NOW.

Lumentum was the first photonics stock I bought back at the beginning of the year, and with time it's only gotten more attractive.

In this massive drawdown, I started to question whether I should really be holding as many names as I do, which to cut, which are forever longs. $LITE is one of the names I want to still own five years from now.

What makes it so special:

Most companies on this floor solve interconnect at one distance and defend it. Lumentum shows up at all three, chip to chip, rack to rack, and building to building, with the same object every time: a semiconductor laser grown on indium phosphide.

It owns the fabs that grow them, which gives them a leg up in this industry, and it's why I file this as a light source company and not a module maker.

It's also the reason a future headed into co-packaged optics doesn't scare me here; rather, it's an opportunity. As optics move closer to the chip, the module shrinks, and the light source grows. Lumentum meets it as a mix shift toward its best margin.

Anyone with capital can rack GPUs; the number of companies that can make an indium phosphide laser at volume is very close to two.

Their financials look stellar: 

Q3 FY2026 (ended 28 March 2026)

Revenue: $808.4M, +90% YoY
Non-GAAP gross margin: 47.9%, +1,270 bps YoY
Adjusted EBITDA: $293.5M, 4.1x a year ago
GAAP net income: $144.2M
Cash and investments: $3.17B
Q4 guide: $960M to $1,010M, operating margin 35-36%

Two fiscal years ago this company lost $546M, now it's a completely different story.
